notes.front: What is Zulu time?
notes.back: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the single time standard used in aviation; times in weather reports end in Z.
notes.explanation: Every weather report and forecast time is in UTC, not local time, so you must convert before comparing with your planned flight.
notes.example: ‘161753Z’ in a weather report is the 16th day of the month at 1753 UTC.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 18

notes.front: What is a METAR, in one sentence?
notes.back: An aviation routine weather report: an observation of current surface weather at an airport, in a standard international format.
notes.explanation: It is the basic ‘what is the weather now’ report for an airport, issued hourly, and the building block of most other products.
notes.example: ‘METAR KINK 121845Z …’ is Wink, Texas, on the 12th at 1845Z.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 15; AIM para. 7-1-28 (“METAR-hourly”)

notes.front: What is a SPECI?
notes.back: A special weather report issued between routine METARs to update them for rapidly changing weather, a mishap or other critical information.
notes.explanation: It uses the same format as a METAR, so it is decoded the same way.
notes.example: ‘SPECI KMDW 121856Z …’ is a special report from Chicago Midway at 1856Z, between hourly reports.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: What is the dew point?
notes.back: The temperature to which air must cool to become saturated, so that it can hold no more moisture.
notes.explanation: When the temperature falls to the dew point, moisture condenses as fog, dew, frost, cloud or precipitation; METARs report both figures.
notes.example: With a temperature of 18 °C and a dew point of 17 °C, the air is almost saturated; fog or low cloud is likely.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Temperature/Dew Point Relationship”, p. 25

notes.front: In aviation weather, what is a ceiling?
notes.back: The lowest broken or overcast layer, or, if fog or haze hides the sky, the vertical visibility (how far up you can see into it).
notes.explanation: Scattered or few clouds do not form a ceiling, however low; that distinction decides many weather questions.
notes.example: Scattered cloud at 700 ft and a broken layer at 1,500 ft: the ceiling is the broken layer at 1,500 ft.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Ceiling”, p. 28

notes.front: What is a TAF, in one sentence?
notes.back: A terminal aerodrome forecast: a forecast for the area within 5 statute miles of an airport, using METAR codes.
notes.explanation: It tells you what to expect at an airport during your planned operation, rather than what is happening now.
notes.example: ‘TAF KPIR 111130Z 1112/1212 …’ is the forecast for Pierre, South Dakota, issued at 1130Z on the 11th.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 18

notes.front: What are ASOS and AWOS?
notes.back: ASOS (Automated Surface Observing System) and AWOS (Automated Weather Observing System): automated airport weather stations reporting continuously, broadcast by radio.
notes.explanation: US airport METARs and SPECIs come from automated observing systems, and the broadcasts can be heard by radio near the airport.
notes.example: Jamestown Regional’s data block lists ‘ASOS 118.425’: tune it to hear the current observation.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: What is ATIS?
notes.back: Automated Terminal Information Service: a looped recording of local weather and other non-control airport information, broadcast on a local frequency.
notes.explanation: It is normally updated hourly, so it is a quick source of an airport’s current conditions.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS)”, p. 67

notes.front: What is a Convective SIGMET?
notes.back: A SIGMET (significant meteorological information) for convection: severe storms, lines of storms, or storms hidden inside other cloud (embedded).
notes.explanation: It flags the most dangerous convective weather, which a remote PIC should avoid when planning.
notes.example: A Convective SIGMET for a line of storms across your county is a clear reason to postpone.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Convective Significant Meteorological Information (WST)”, p. 19

notes.front: What is the Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA)?
notes.back: An Aviation Weather Center website showing observations, forecasts and warnings for the continental US on one map.
notes.explanation: It gathers clouds, precipitation, thunderstorms, wind and more into a single picture of weather that may affect a flight.
notes.example: Selecting the ‘CIG/VIS’ tab shows forecast ceilings and visibility across your region.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-4, “Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA)”

notes.front: What is a surface analysis chart?
notes.back: A chart of current surface weather: pressure highs and lows, fronts (boundaries between air masses), and station temperatures, dew points, winds and weather.
notes.explanation: Weather charts give the overall picture of weather systems, which is where flight planning should begin.
notes.example: A cold front drawn across Kansas on the surface analysis tells you what may reach Missouri later.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 13, “Surface Analysis Chart”, p. 13-13

notes.front: What is a weather depiction chart?
notes.back: A chart built from METARs and other surface observations, outlining areas of low ceilings and poor visibility across the country.
notes.explanation: It shows at a glance where conditions are poor, before you look at individual reports.
notes.example: A hatched area over the Ohio Valley marks ceilings under 1,000 ft with visibility under 3 miles.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 13, “Weather Depiction Chart”, p. 13-15

notes.front: What is a low-level significant weather prognostic chart?
notes.back: A forecast chart of aviation weather hazards from the surface to 24,000 ft, mainly for briefing pilots flying by sight.
notes.explanation: ‘Prognostic’ means forecast: it shows where hazardous weather is expected, not where it is now.
notes.example: Use it to see whether a front and its weather are forecast over your site tomorrow.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 13, “Significant Weather Prognostic Charts”, p. 13-15

notes.front: In a METAR or TAF, what are sky condition codes?
notes.back: Contractions for how much of the sky a cloud layer covers, in eighths, followed by the layer’s base in hundreds of feet.
notes.explanation: The AIM key lists SKC, FEW, SCT, BKN and OVC for amount, CLR (clear below 12,000 ft, automated reports only), VV for vertical visibility, and CB or TCU for cloud type.
notes.example: ‘OVC012CB’ is an overcast layer of cumulonimbus with its base at 1,200 ft.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”

notes.front: In a METAR or TAF, what are weather codes?
notes.back: Short codes for significant weather, written in the order intensity or proximity, descriptor, precipitation, obscuration, other.
notes.explanation: A “-” means light, no sign moderate and “+” heavy; VC means in the vicinity. Descriptors such as TS and SH come before precipitation such as RA.
notes.example: The AIM decodes ‘-RA FG’ as light rain and fog.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”

notes.front: In a METAR, what are report modifiers and remarks?
notes.back: Modifiers after the time say how the report was made (AUTO, COR); remarks at the end, starting with RMK, add detail.
notes.explanation: When AUTO appears, the remarks also encode the type of sensor equipment at the station (AO1 or AO2).
notes.example: In the AIM’s sample report from Pittsburgh, COR after the time marks a corrected report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”; Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 3a (AO1, AO2)
introduces: report modifiers and remarks (AUTO, COR, RMK, AO1, AO2, PRESFR, PRESRR)
uses: report modifiers and remarks (AUTO, COR, RMK, AO1, AO2, PRESFR, PRESRR)

notes.front: What is runway visual range (RVR)?
notes.back: The visual range along a runway, measured in the touchdown zone and reported in a METAR in feet after the visibility.
notes.explanation: It tells pilots how far down the runway they can see when visibility is poor. In a METAR the group starts with R and the runway number.
notes.example: The AIM reads one such group as “runway three two left R-V-R one thousand two hundred”.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”

notes.front: In a METAR, what is the wind group?
notes.back: The true direction the wind blows from, in tens of degrees (or VRB if variable), then its speed, with KT for knots.
notes.explanation: If the wind is gusty, a G follows the speed, then the highest gust.
notes.example: The AIM decodes ‘VRB04KT’ as wind variable in direction at 4 knots.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”

notes.front: In a TAF, what are change groups?
notes.back: Groups that mark forecast changes within the valid period, each starting with a code such as FM or TEMPO.
notes.explanation: The AIM key lists FM (from), TEMPO (temporary), BECMG (becoming) and PROB30 or PROB40 (a 30 or 40 percent probability).
notes.example: ‘TEMPO 0920/0922’ forecasts temporary changes between 2000Z and 2200Z on the 9th.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
introduces: TAF change groups (FM, TEMPO, BECMG, PROB30, PROB40)

notes.front: Which website does AC 107-2A encourage remote PICs to use for a Flight Service weather briefing?
notes.back: 1800wxbrief.com; a free account is needed.
notes.explanation: Flight Service is the FAA’s briefing service; its online self-briefing suits remote pilots.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.3, p. B-2

notes.front: Should a remote pilot use Flight Service’s telephone briefing?
notes.back: No: AC 107-2A says the telephone service is intended for manned aircraft pilots only.
notes.explanation: Remote pilots are pointed to the online service instead.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.3, p. B-2

notes.front: Which free website, needing no registration, offers METARs and TAFs?
notes.back: The National Weather Service’s Aviation Weather Center, aviationweather.gov.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A says it offers all the weather products important to a remote PIC.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.3.1, p. B-2

notes.front: While reviewing the weather, which FAA website should you also check for TFRs?
notes.back: tfr.faa.gov.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A calls reviewing TFRs critical during the same preflight review.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.3.1, p. B-2

notes.front: What caution does the AIM give about weather from third-party vendors or unfamiliar products?
notes.back: They may not meet FAA/NWS quality standards; check what the product is, how current it is and whether it is relevant.
notes.explanation: When in doubt, the AIM says to consult a Flight Service specialist.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-3, “Use of Aviation Weather Products”

notes.front: In a METAR, what does the K in KGGG mean?
notes.back: It is the prefix for the 48 contiguous states; GGG is the airport’s identifier.
notes.explanation: Station identifiers are four-letter ICAO codes; outside the contiguous states the first letters show the region.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: Which letters begin Alaskan and Hawaiian station identifiers?
notes.back: PA for Alaska and PH for Hawaii.
notes.explanation: In the 48 contiguous states, identifiers begin with K.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: In a METAR, what does the group 161753Z mean?
notes.back: The 16th day of the month, at 1753 UTC.
notes.explanation: The first two digits are the date, the last four the time, always in Zulu time.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: In a METAR, what do AUTO and COR mean?
notes.back: AUTO: from an automated station with no human intervention. COR: a corrected report replacing one with an error.
notes.explanation: When an observer augments an automated station, AUTO is dropped.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: report modifiers and remarks (AUTO, COR, RMK, AO1, AO2, PRESFR, PRESRR)

notes.front: In a METAR, what does 14021G26KT mean?
notes.back: Wind from 140° true at 21 knots, gusting to 26 knots.
notes.explanation: The first three digits are the direction the wind blows from, in tens of degrees; G gives the peak gust.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: In a METAR wind group, what do VRB and 00000KT mean?
notes.back: VRB: variable direction. 00000KT: calm.
notes.explanation: If the direction varies by 60° or more, the extremes are added, e.g. 180V260.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”

notes.front: In a METAR, how is visibility reported, for example 3/4SM?
notes.back: As prevailing visibility in statute miles and fractions: 3/4SM is three-quarters of a statute mile.
notes.explanation: Part 107 compares visibility with its 3 statute mile minimum, so this group matters.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: In a METAR, what does R17L/1400FT mean?
notes.back: Runway visual range: 1,400 ft along runway 17 left.
notes.explanation: RVR is how far a pilot can see down the runway, reported after the prevailing visibility.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: In METAR weather groups, what do ‘-’, no sign and ‘+’ mean?
notes.back: Light, moderate and heavy.
notes.explanation: So +TSRA is a thunderstorm with heavy rain.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: In a METAR, what does VC before a weather code mean?
notes.back: In the vicinity: 5 to 10 statute miles from the point of observation, not at the airport.
notes.explanation: VCTS, for example, is a thunderstorm nearby rather than overhead.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: weather codes (VC, TS, SH, FZ, RA, GR, FC, BR, FG, HZ, FU)

notes.front: In METAR weather codes, what do TS, SH and RA mean?
notes.back: Thunderstorm, showers and rain.
notes.explanation: TS and SH are descriptors; RA is a precipitation type, so SHRA is rain showers.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: weather codes (VC, TS, SH, FZ, RA, GR, FC, BR, FG, HZ, FU)

notes.front: In METAR weather codes, what do HZ and FU mean?
notes.back: Haze and smoke.
notes.explanation: Both are obscurations: they reduce visibility without being precipitation.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: weather codes (VC, TS, SH, FZ, RA, GR, FC, BR, FG, HZ, FU)

notes.front: In METAR weather codes, what do FZ and GR mean?
notes.back: Freezing and hail.
notes.explanation: FZRA, for example, is freezing rain.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: weather codes (VC, TS, SH, FZ, RA, GR, FC, BR, FG, HZ, FU)

notes.front: In METAR weather codes, what do FC and +FC mean?
notes.back: FC: funnel cloud. +FC: tornado or waterspout.
notes.explanation: Both are listed under ‘Other’ weather phenomena in the METAR key.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: weather codes (VC, TS, SH, FZ, RA, GR, FC, BR, FG, HZ, FU)

notes.front: In a METAR sky group such as BKN008, what units is 008 in?
notes.back: Hundreds of feet above ground level: 800 ft AGL.
notes.explanation: Cloud heights are always AGL in METARs, which makes them easy to compare with a drone’s height.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 17

notes.front: In a METAR or TAF, FEW means {{c1::more than 0/8 up to 2/8 of the sky covered}}.
notes.explanation: Sky cover is reported in eighths of the sky.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: sky condition codes (SKC, CLR, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC, VV, CB, TCU)

notes.front: In a METAR or TAF, SCT means {{c1::scattered: 3/8 to 4/8 of the sky covered}}.
notes.explanation: Scattered cloud does not form a ceiling.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: sky condition codes (SKC, CLR, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC, VV, CB, TCU)

notes.front: In a METAR or TAF, BKN means {{c1::broken: 5/8 to 7/8 of the sky covered}}.
notes.explanation: The lowest broken layer can be a ceiling.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: sky condition codes (SKC, CLR, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC, VV, CB, TCU)

notes.front: In a METAR or TAF, OVC means {{c1::overcast: 8/8, the whole sky covered}}.
notes.explanation: The lowest overcast layer can be a ceiling.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: sky condition codes (SKC, CLR, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC, VV, CB, TCU)

notes.front: In a METAR, what do SKC and CLR mean?
notes.back: SKC: sky clear. CLR, used only in automated reports: clear below 12,000 ft.
notes.explanation: Automated stations do not detect or report clouds above 12,000 ft.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: sky condition codes (SKC, CLR, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC, VV, CB, TCU)

notes.front: In a METAR, what does VV003 mean?
notes.back: Sky obscured, with vertical visibility of 300 ft; this counts as a ceiling.
notes.explanation: Vertical visibility is reported when fog or another obscuration hides the sky.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”

notes.front: In a METAR, what do CB and TCU after a cloud layer mean?
notes.back: Cumulonimbus and towering cumulus.
notes.explanation: They are reported with the height of their layer, e.g. OVC012CB.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 17
uses: sky condition codes (SKC, CLR, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC, VV, CB, TCU)

notes.front: In a METAR, what does 18/17 mean, and what would M05 mean?
notes.back: Temperature 18 °C, dew point 17 °C. M means minus, so M05 is −5 °C.
notes.explanation: Temperature and dew point are always in degrees Celsius.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 17

notes.front: In a METAR, what does A2970 mean?
notes.back: Altimeter setting 29.70 inches of mercury: the local pressure pilots set on their altimeters.
notes.explanation: It always follows the letter A and is a four-digit group.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 17

notes.front: In a METAR’s remarks, what do PRESFR and PRESRR mean?
notes.back: Pressure falling rapidly, and pressure rising rapidly.
notes.explanation: Remarks always begin with RMK and can include wind, visibility and pressure details.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 17
uses: report modifiers and remarks (AUTO, COR, RMK, AO1, AO2, PRESFR, PRESRR)

notes.front: In a METAR’s remarks, what is the difference between AO1 and AO2?
notes.back: AO2 stations have a precipitation discriminator (telling liquid from frozen precipitation); AO1 stations do not.
notes.explanation: Both mark automated stations.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”
uses: report modifiers and remarks (AUTO, COR, RMK, AO1, AO2, PRESFR, PRESRR)

notes.front: How long is a TAF valid, and when are scheduled TAFs issued?
notes.back: For 24 or 30 hours; issued four times a day, at 0000, 0600, 1200 and 1800Z.
notes.explanation: TAFs are usually issued for larger airports.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 18

notes.front: In a TAF, what does the valid-period group 0812/0912 mean?
notes.back: Valid from 1200Z on the 8th to 1200Z on the 9th.
notes.explanation: Each four-digit half is a date then an hour, in UTC.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 18

notes.front: In a TAF, what does a FM group (e.g. FM091930) introduce?
notes.back: A rapid, significant change: from that time (here 1930Z on the 9th), the conditions that follow apply.
notes.explanation: Each FM group starts a new line; don’t confuse FM100000 (0000Z on the 10th) with 1000Z.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: TAF change groups (FM, TEMPO, BECMG, PROB30, PROB40)

notes.front: In a TAF, what does TEMPO mean?
notes.back: Temporary fluctuations in the stated period, each expected to last less than an hour.
notes.explanation: The main forecast still describes the prevailing conditions around the TEMPO spells.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 19
uses: TAF change groups (FM, TEMPO, BECMG, PROB30, PROB40)

notes.front: In a TAF, what does BECMG mean?
notes.back: Becoming: a change expected to take place during the stated period.
notes.explanation: NWS TAFs do not use BECMG, but you will meet it elsewhere, including the testing supplement’s KOKC TAF.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: TAF change groups (FM, TEMPO, BECMG, PROB30, PROB40)

notes.front: In a TAF, what does PROB30 mean?
notes.back: A 30 percent probability of the stated conditions during the given period (PROB40: 40 percent).
notes.explanation: It is commonly used for the chance of thunderstorms and precipitation.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: TAF change groups (FM, TEMPO, BECMG, PROB30, PROB40)

notes.front: In a TAF, what does P6SM mean?
notes.back: Visibility forecast to be greater than 6 statute miles.
notes.explanation: ‘P’ stands for plus.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 19

notes.front: Which cloud type does a TAF name in its sky groups?
notes.back: Only cumulonimbus (CB); METARs also report towering cumulus (TCU).
notes.explanation: Otherwise TAF sky groups use the same format as METARs.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 19
uses: sky condition codes (SKC, CLR, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC, VV, CB, TCU)

notes.front: In a US TAF, what does WS010/31022KT mean?
notes.back: Low-level wind shear (a sudden change of wind with height) at 1,000 ft, with wind from 310° at 22 knots above.
notes.explanation: It forecasts non-convective wind shear at or below 2,000 ft.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”

notes.front: What is a TAF AMD?
notes.back: An amended TAF, replacing the routine forecast.
notes.explanation: Always check the issue time to be sure you have the latest forecast.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 18

notes.front: How often is an ASOS/AWOS radio broadcast updated?
notes.back: Every minute: a 20–30 second weather message, updated each minute.
notes.explanation: That makes it the most current weather you can hear at an airport.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: Up to what distance and height are ASOS/AWOS radio broadcasts designed to be received?
notes.back: Up to 25 NM from the site and 10,000 ft AGL.
notes.explanation: Local conditions may limit reception; many sites also offer the same message by telephone.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: Which modifier does a METAR from an ASOS/AWOS carry when no human has added to it?
notes.back: AUTO.
notes.explanation: When an observer augments or backs up the station, the AUTO modifier disappears.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”
uses: report modifiers and remarks (AUTO, COR, RMK, AO1, AO2, PRESFR, PRESRR)

notes.front: Can you talk to an AWOS on its frequency?
notes.back: No: there is no two-way communication capability.
notes.explanation: You simply monitor the frequency for the automated broadcast.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-A reports {{c1::only the altimeter setting}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-AV reports {{c1::the altimeter setting and visibility}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-1 usually reports {{c1::the altimeter setting, wind, temperature, dew point and density altitude}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-2 reports {{c1::everything AWOS-1 reports, plus visibility}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-3 reports {{c1::everything AWOS-2 reports, plus cloud and ceiling data}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-3P reports {{c1::everything AWOS-3 reports, plus precipitation identification}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-3T reports {{c1::everything AWOS-3 reports, plus thunderstorm and lightning reporting}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-3PT reports {{c1::everything AWOS-3P reports, plus thunderstorm and lightning reporting}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: AWOS-4 reports {{c1::everything AWOS-3 reports, plus sensors for precipitation, freezing rain, thunderstorms and runway surface}}.
notes.explanation: AWOS systems are classified into nine levels according to what they report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: How often is ATIS normally updated, and how can you tell it has changed?
notes.back: Normally once an hour, or more often if conditions change; each update gets a new code letter (Alpha, then Bravo…).
notes.explanation: The letter lets pilots confirm they have the current recording.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS)”, p. 67

notes.front: Besides the weather, what does an ATIS broadcast include?
notes.back: Runways in use, specific ATC procedures, and construction that could affect taxiing.
notes.explanation: ATIS is non-control information: it informs rather than instructs.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS)”, p. 67

notes.front: When does a sectional’s airport data block show an ASOS/AWOS frequency?
notes.back: When full-time ATIS is not available at the airport.
notes.explanation: So an ASOS/AWOS frequency in a data block tells you that is where to hear the airport’s current weather.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: Which conditions lead to a Convective SIGMET?
notes.back: Severe thunderstorms with surface winds over 50 knots, surface hail of ¾ inch or more, or tornadoes; also embedded or lines of thunderstorms.
notes.explanation: It is also issued for thunderstorms with heavy precipitation covering 40% or more of a region of 3,000 square miles or more.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Convective Significant Meteorological Information (WST)”, p. 19

notes.front: Over what time span can the GFA display weather?
notes.back: From 14 hours in the past to 15 hours in the future.
notes.explanation: Its observation tabs show the current time and the previous 14 hours.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-4, “Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA)”

notes.front: Which legacy text product is the GFA designed to replace?
notes.back: The area forecast (FA).
notes.explanation: Older study material, including the Study Guide, still describes the area forecast.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-4, “Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA)”

notes.front: At what stage of planning should weather charts be used?
notes.back: At the beginning, for an overall picture of weather systems and fronts.
notes.explanation: Surface analysis, weather depiction and prognostic charts give the big picture; reports and forecasts give the detail.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 13, “Weather Charts”, p. 13-13

notes.front: How often is the surface analysis chart transmitted?
notes.back: Every 3 hours.
notes.explanation: It covers the contiguous 48 states and adjacent areas.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 13, “Surface Analysis Chart”, p. 13-13

notes.front: On the little weather plot drawn at each station on a surface analysis, what are a short barb, a long barb and a pennant worth?
notes.back: 5 knots, 10 knots and 50 knots.
notes.explanation: The line the barbs hang from shows the true direction the wind blows from.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 13, “Surface Analysis Chart”, p. 13-13

notes.front: On a weather depiction chart, what does a hatched area outlined by a smooth line show?
notes.back: Ceilings below 1,000 ft and visibility below 3 miles.
notes.explanation: A non-hatched outlined area shows ceilings of 1,000–3,000 ft and visibility of 3–5 miles; better areas are not outlined.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 13, “Weather Depiction Chart”, p. 13-15

notes.front: A remote PIC wants a preflight weather briefing. Which route does AC 107-2A recommend?
notes.back: Flight Service online, at 1800wxbrief.com.
notes.choices:
A) Phone Flight Service for a standard briefing
B) Brief online at 1800wxbrief.com
C) Call the nearest control tower
notes.choicesExplained: A: AC 107-2A says the telephone service is intended for manned aircraft pilots only. C: AC 107-2A points remote pilots to Flight Service online and the Aviation Weather Center, not to control towers.
notes.explanation: Flight Service’s telephone service is intended for manned aircraft pilots.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.3, p. B-2

notes.front: A METAR is timed 121845Z. When was the observation made?
notes.back: On the 12th day of the month at 18:45 UTC.
notes.explanation: Convert UTC to local time before comparing it with your planned flight.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.back: No. It has only scattered layers, at 700 ft and 25,000 ft; a ceiling needs a broken or overcast layer or vertical visibility.

notes.back: Ceiling 700 ft AGL overcast; visibility 1½ SM in moderate rain.
notes.explanation: OVC007 is overcast at 700 ft; RA with no sign is moderate rain.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 12

notes.front: Figure: SPECI KMDW. What kind of report is this, and why are such reports issued?
notes.back: A special report (SPECI), issued between routine METARs to report rapidly changing weather, a mishap or other critical information.
notes.explanation: It is decoded exactly like a METAR.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

image.alt: A special report from the testing supplement, wrapped over three lines: ‘SPECI KMDW 121856Z’ / ‘32005KT 1 1/2SM RA OVC007’ / ‘17/16 A2980 RMK RAB35’.
image.credit: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, figure 12

notes.front: Figure: SPECI KJFK. What are the visibility and ceiling?
notes.back: Visibility ½ SM in fog; ceiling 500 ft overcast.
notes.explanation: R04/2200 adds a runway visual range of 2,200 ft on runway 04.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 12

image.alt: A special report from the testing supplement, wrapped over three lines: ‘SPECI KJFK 121853Z’ / ‘18004KT 1/2SM FG R04/2200’ / ‘OVC005 20/18 A3006’.
image.credit: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, figure 12

notes.front: Figure: SPECI KJFK. Could a remote pilot operate under part 107 at this airport’s location in these conditions?
notes.back: No. Visibility is ½ SM, and part 107 requires at least 3 SM flight visibility from the control station.
notes.explanation: With a 500 ft ceiling, staying 500 ft below the cloud would also leave no room to fly.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.51, “Operating limitations for small unmanned aircraft” (eCFR, current as of 2026-09-25)

image.alt: A special report from the testing supplement, wrapped over three lines: ‘SPECI KJFK 121853Z’ / ‘18004KT 1/2SM FG R04/2200’ / ‘OVC005 20/18 A3006’.
image.credit: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, figure 12

notes.front: Figure: METAR KLAX. The temperature is 16 °C and the dew point 15 °C. What does this suggest?
notes.back: The air is nearly saturated, so mist, fog or low cloud is likely; the report already shows mist (BR).
notes.explanation: When temperature and dew point are close, fog, low clouds and precipitation are highly likely.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Methods by Which Air Reaches the Saturation Point”, p. 25
uses: weather codes (VC, TS, SH, FZ, RA, GR, FC, BR, FG, HZ, FU)

notes.front: Figure: TAF KOKC. When was it issued, and for what period is it valid?
notes.back: Issued at 1130Z on the 5th; valid from 1200Z on the 5th to 1800Z on the 6th, 30 hours.
notes.explanation: 0512/0618 reads as day-hour to day-hour, in UTC.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 15

notes.back: Visibility 1½ SM in mist.
notes.explanation: TEMPO 0513/0516 marks temporary fluctuations within that window, each lasting under an hour.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 15

notes.back: Wind 180° at 10 knots, visibility over 6 SM, sky clear.
notes.explanation: FM051600 starts a new set of conditions at 1600Z on the 5th.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 15

notes.explanation: TSRA with no sign is a thunderstorm with moderate rain.

notes.front: You plan a job 3 miles from an airport tomorrow afternoon. Which product gives the airport’s forecast for then?
notes.back: Its TAF, which covers the area within 5 SM of the airport for 24 or 30 hours.
notes.explanation: A METAR only shows current weather.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 18

notes.front: An airport near your site has no tower and no ATIS. Its data block lists ‘ASOS 118.425’. How can you get its current weather?
notes.back: Listen to the ASOS broadcast on 118.425, updated every minute.
notes.explanation: Data blocks show ASOS/AWOS frequencies where full-time ATIS is not available.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: At 1400 the ATIS was ‘Information Charlie’; at 1500 it is ‘Information Delta’. What happened?
notes.back: The recording was updated, as normally happens each hour, and given the next code letter.
notes.explanation: A new letter tells you the information may have changed.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS)”, p. 67

notes.front: A thunderstorm begins at an airport at 1856Z, between routine reports, and a report is issued at once. What type of report is it?
notes.back: A SPECI.
notes.explanation: Routine METARs follow a schedule; SPECIs are issued in between when weather changes.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16; AIM para. 7-1-28, TBL 7-1-1

notes.front: A Convective SIGMET is in force over your area for a line of thunderstorms. What should a remote PIC do?
notes.back: Treat it as a serious hazard warning and postpone or relocate the operation.
notes.explanation: Convective SIGMETs warn of severe thunderstorms, hail, tornadoes and lines of storms.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Convective Significant Meteorological Information (WST)”, p. 19

notes.front: METAR versus TAF: what does each give you?
notes.back: METAR: observed weather now. TAF: forecast weather for the next 24 or 30 hours, within 5 SM of the airport.
notes.explanation: They share the same codes, so decoding one teaches the other.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 18

notes.front: Is wind direction true or magnetic in a METAR, and in ATIS or ASOS/AWOS voice broadcasts?
notes.back: METAR (written): true north. ATIS and ASOS/AWOS radio broadcasts: magnetic north.
notes.explanation: The difference between the two is the local magnetic variation.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: In a METAR, what separates BR from FG?
notes.back: Visibility: BR (mist) is 5/8 SM or more; FG (fog) is below 5/8 SM.
notes.explanation: Both are obscurations; the code tells you how badly visibility is reduced.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-28, “Key to Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”
uses: weather codes (VC, TS, SH, FZ, RA, GR, FC, BR, FG, HZ, FU)

notes.front: In a TAF, how does TEMPO differ from FM?
notes.back: FM: a lasting change from a set time. TEMPO: brief fluctuations, each under an hour, within a period.
notes.explanation: After a TEMPO period the earlier conditions still apply; after FM, the new ones do.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)”, p. 19
uses: TAF change groups (FM, TEMPO, BECMG, PROB30, PROB40)

notes.front: METAR versus SPECI: what is the difference?
notes.back: A METAR is the routine scheduled report; a SPECI is a special report issued between them when weather changes rapidly.
notes.explanation: Both use the same format.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3a, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”, p. 16

notes.front: Scattered versus broken cloud: which can form a ceiling, and why?
notes.back: Only broken (5/8–7/8) or overcast layers form a ceiling; scattered (3/8–4/8) never does.
notes.explanation: A ceiling is defined as the lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Ceiling”, p. 28
